messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: copula stuff
parts:
I cleaned up the attached example of a copula (family of multivariate CDFs for dependent standard uniform marginals) that I posted the other day. And every continuous joint density has a unique decomposition into a copula density (evaluated at the CDFs of the margins) and the product of the marginal PDFs.

1) What is the protocol for pushing into the example-models repo? I think it should just require that the example runs, but I haven't pushed it yet.

2) We should get a grant from some finance company to implement a bunch of copula stuff in Stan.

3) Can nomad specialize in a clever way to autodifferentiate a K-dimensional CDF when there is no explicit form for the PDF? If it takes at least 2^K stack allocations, then I guess it would only be useful for small K, in which case someone has probably derived the PDF explicitly.

4) The example of a Clayton copula is useful for testing because it illustrates what can go wrong with just 3 parameters (two standard normals and a Kendall's tau). For non-zero values of the Kendall's tau, the two normals have increasing dependence in their lower tails only. Since the parameter dependence is not constant, NUTS has a non-trivial percentage of iterations where n_divergent__ != 0.

But you can manipulate the extent of the problems under NUTS with a prior on the Kendall's tau, such as a symmetric beta distribution on (-1,1) with a shape parameter alpha. If alpha = 3, then the Rhats are small whether in the original scale or in ranks. But divergence happens on about 1/3 of the iterations, so as Michael would say, you should wait for the Riemannian stuff.

For alpha <= 8, it appears that I would reject the null hypothesis that all the half-chains have the same distribution no matter how long the chains run. This is because any chain has a small probability of getting stuck briefly in the lower tail of the normals, and when that happens for some chains but not others, that is enough to reject the null. But the first two moments are right for each margin, so as Andrew would say, there would be little substantive harm if you decided that convergence had occurred.

For alpha = 8.25, 18% of the iterations diverge, and I would fail to reject the null hypothesis that all the chains have the same distribution, even with a million iterations. In other words, alpha = 8 is right near the tipping point, and as I would say, we can distinguish empirically between nonconvergence and convergence to the stationary distribution, even when geometric ergodicity does not hold.

I added an option to the pairs plot where you can split according to an arbitrary condition, rather than just putting the first few chains below the diagonal and the rest of the chains above. Here the split is according to whether tau is more than one standard deviation from zero (given that alpha = 8.25). If not, you basically have independent normals. If so, you have noticeable lower tail dependence.

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] copula stuff
parts:
On Monday, August 25, 2014 1:05:24 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> 3) Can nomad specialize in a clever way to autodifferentiate a K-dimensional CDF when there is no explicit form for the PDF? If it takes at least 2^K stack allocations, then I guess it would only be useful for small K, in which case someone has probably derived the PDF explicitly.

I didn't understand the question.  You mean autodifferentiate an
iterative algorithm to compute the CDF?  Michael's leery of this working
in general, but we found it works well enough for sampling in many cases
(like differentiating the integrator in the ode solver).

It is kind of like the ODE thing but going the other way. In the case of a copula, we know the explicit form of the multivariate CDF of the marginal uniforms

F(u_1, u_2, ..., u_d | theta)

but for Stan's purposes we need the (logarithm of the) copula density function, which is

dF(u_1, u_2, ..., u_d | theta)
------------------------------ = f(u_1, u_2, ..., u_d | theta)
du_1,du_2,...,du_d


but for large d, there is sometimes no explicit form of f(u_1, u_2, ..., u_d | theta). So, loosely speaking, it would be great if we could evaluate

var f_log(var_vector u, var theta) {
  const int d = u.rows();
  var p = F(u, theta);
  var dp_du_1 = get_partial(p, u[1]);
  var dp_du_1_du_2 = get_partial(dp_du_1, u[2]);
  /* more of these */
  var log_density = log(get_partial(dp_du_*, u[d]);
  return log_density;
}

and then be able to differentiate that with respect to theta and whatever other unknowns there are to do HMC. But the above "implementation" would only work for fixed d unless there is some metaprogramming magic, and even then it would stack overflow for large d if we had to reserve 2^d spaces on the stack. So, I don't know if there is some way of specializing the var class in nomad to do that in a space-efficient way.
Is the pairs plot part of RStan?  If not, it should be.

The old implementation is. I haven't pushed the new one yet.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] copula stuff
parts:
We can do this with second-order autodiff. But it's
not going to be super efficient in high dimensions, because
each dimension is going to involve a forward pass on the
function F.

The get_partial() operation you have will be a forward-mode
auto-diff d_ value. That can then be logged, or whatever,
and autodiffed through for HMC.

If the F doesn't involve any pdf or cdf calls in Stan,
could do it now. Otherwise, we're going to have to wait
until the 2nd order autodiff is completed. It's held up
on Windows testing at the moment.

Are there a fixed number of these, or do people write their
own F?

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] copula stuff

On Tuesday, August 26, 2014 9:55:24 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
If the F doesn't involve any pdf or cdf calls in Stan,
could do it now.  Otherwise, we're going to have to wait
until the 2nd order autodiff is completed.  It's held up
on Windows testing at the moment.

Are there a fixed number of these, or do people write their
own F?

Very cool. I think it could wait a bit. There are potentially an infinite number of copula CDFs but in practice, people can only use the ones that have an explicit copula density function for estimation. But also in practice, they estimate the parameters of each margin separately and then pretend those estimates are fixed when they estimate the copula part. Full Bayesian estimation would be much better if we could make it feasible in high dimensions.

Ben

- Bob
